content: Fungating wounds are a result of primary, secondary, or recurrent malignant diseases and are commonly associated with advanced stages of cancer. While a small number of patients may achieve wound healing through surgical excision, the majority of cases require palliative care. The primary goals of managing fungating wounds are to slow the progression of the disease and improve the patient’s quality of life. This is achieved by addressing physical symptoms such as excessive exudate, unpleasant odor, pain, and the risk of bleeding. The selection of appropriate dressings and topical agents plays a critical role in achieving these objectives. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of dressings and topical agents on the quality of life and symptom management in individuals with fungating malignant wounds. The search for relevant studies was updated in August 2013 and included databases such as the Wounds Group Specialised Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or, in their absence, controlled clinical trials (CCTs) with a concurrent control group. Four trials involving a total of 164 participants were included in the review. The first trial, conducted in women with superficial breast lesions, compared a 6% miltefosine solution to a placebo. The results indicated that miltefosine significantly delayed tumor progression, with a median time to treatment failure of 56 days in the miltefosine group compared to 21 days in the placebo group (p = 0.007, log-rank test). The second trial evaluated the use of topical metronidazole compared to a placebo. However, the results up to the point of cross-over were not statistically significant, and no definitive conclusions could be drawn. The third trial assessed the effectiveness of foam dressings containing silver versus foam dressings without silver. It was found that a greater number of patients experienced a reduction in malodor when using the foam dressings with silver compared to those without silver (p = 0.049). The fourth trial compared manuka honey-coated dressings to nanocrystalline silver-coated dressings. This study found no statistically significant differences between the two types of dressings in terms of exudate, malodor, or wound pain. Despite these findings, all four trials had notable methodological limitations, which weaken the reliability of the evidence. The authors concluded that there is weak evidence from one small trial suggesting that a 6% miltefosine solution may slow disease progression in patients with superficial fungating breast lesions who have previously undergone radiotherapy, surgery, hormonal therapy, or chemotherapy. Additionally, there is weak evidence indicating that foam dressings containing silver may help reduce malodor. However, there is insufficient evidence to provide clear guidance on improving quality of life or managing symptoms associated with fungating wounds. Further research is necessary to establish more robust evidence in this area.
